newsitem.title: USA: Israel presses Palestinians on violence.
newsitem.headline: Israel presses Palestinians on violence.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's personal representative said on Tuesday that Palestinians have to do more to control violence before peace talks can resume.

"We need to be sure the Palestinians are meeting their obligations to fight violence and not incite violence," Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said after meeting U.S. Middle East Coordinator Dennis Ross at the State Department.
"Unfortunately, what we see is a lack of real effort by the Palestinian side," he told reporters.
Israel has "clear evidence that Palestinian police were involved in terrorism against Israelis," he added.
Naveh was in Washington for talks aimed at trying to break a deadlock in Israeli-Palestinian negotiations.
He spoke before Palestinian President Yasser Ararfat and Israeli Foreign Minster David Levy announced in Brussels that they had made progress in bridging their differences.
U.S. officials said they had not had a readout from the Levy-Arafat meeting and so had no immediate comment.
Earlier, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns had indicated U.S. expectations for the Brussels talks -- sponsored by the European Union -- were very low.
"Pulling a meeting together is admirable. It's a good first step. It won't solve the Middle East peace problems, not by a long shot," he said.
Still, he said the United States was in close coordination with the EU negotiator and supported his efforts to arrange the meeting.
On Naveh's charge that Palestinians engaged in terrorism against Israel, Burns rejected any hint that "the entire Palestinian Authority is full of people who want to promote terrorism."
He said Arafat "unequivocally" objected to any association by Palestinian Authority members in any effort to destabilise or plan terrorist attacks against Israel.
And he noted that Arafat had over the weekend arrested four Palestinian Authority officials who are suspected of involvement in plots against Israel.

He drew a distinction between Arafat and his former justice minister, Freih Abu Meddein, who angered the United States and rights groups by campaigning to execute Palestinans who sell land to the Israelis.
On Monday, Burns said Washington would "shed no tears" for Abu Meddein, who then accused Burns of acting like a rude cowboy with a Zionist attitude.

On Tuesday, Burns replied: "Well, I'm proud to be called a vulgar cowboy with a Zionist attitude if, in fact, he's upset with me for calling him someone who has been irresponsible in public office and who doesn't deserve to hold public office."
"We're very pleased he's resigned ... because here's someone who tried to pour oil on the flames and incite violence against Israelis."

Netanyahu said on Monday he was sending Naveh, a senior adviser, to Washington with proposals for ending the four-month-old peacemaking crisis. This follows a trip to Washington last week by Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat.

Israeli-PLO talks, launched with a U.S.-backed interim accord in 1993, have been stuck since Netanyahu started building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March, triggering Palestinian protests.
On the deadlock, Burns said the United States would never give up its mediation efforts but Palestinians and Israel have prime responsibility to revive peace negotiations.

He gave no indication that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright -- who has not visited the Middle East since taking office in January -- would go there ahead of a planned economic summit in Qatar in November.
At the moment, Albright is "fully involved, both in the strategy and tactics (of U.S. peace efforts). I'm not sure what else she can do," he said.
